en.title: Marketing: the whole course
en.short: What a marketing course covers, how it is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What marketing is
sections.text: Marketing is the activity of creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offers that have value for customers, clients, partners and society. It is wider than selling or advertising. Selling begins after a product exists; marketing begins with understanding people and deciding what to offer. A marketing course therefore mixes economics, psychology, statistics and management. You learn how customers behave, how to research them, how to divide a market, how to position an offer, and how to manage product, price, place and promotion. You also learn the limits: marketing must be truthful, respect consumer law, and serve the organisation and its stakeholders over time.

sections.heading: How a marketing degree is usually organised
sections.text: Programmes differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook for length, award and exemptions. In Nigeria, a BSc Marketing at a university commonly runs for four years full time. Polytechnics commonly offer the ND and HND in Marketing, each usually two years full time, with the HND building on the ND. In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree in marketing or business with marketing is commonly three years full time; in the United States, a bachelor’s degree is commonly four years. Master’s programmes are usually one year full time in the United Kingdom and often longer in Nigeria. Professional bodies such as the National Institute of Marketing of Nigeria and the Chartered Institute of Marketing in the United Kingdom offer qualifications and sometimes exemptions. Confirm current rules with the body and your department.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Most courses begin with principles and the marketing environment: the actors and forces outside the firm, such as competitors, customers, technology and regulation, and how they affect decisions. Consumer behaviour comes next, because you need to understand how people buy. Marketing information and research show how to collect evidence. Segmentation, targeting and positioning explain how to choose whom to serve and how to be seen. The introductory sequence usually continues with product and brand basics, pricing fundamentals, distribution channels and retailing, promotion and integrated marketing communication, and marketing arithmetic. The arithmetic matters: market share, margins and break-even are examined in figures.

Core courses include research design and analysis, services marketing, brand management and brand equity, business-to-business marketing, digital and social media marketing, sales management and personal selling, advertising and campaign management, strategy and planning, international marketing, ethics and consumer protection, relationship marketing and customer relationship management, analytics, product development and innovation, pricing strategy, retail and channel management, social marketing, and the marketing plan project. Master’s level adds advanced marketing theory, advanced consumer behaviour, strategic brand management, and research methods for a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study marketing
sections.text:
Study marketing by applying each idea to a real offer. Choose one product or service you know, such as a mobile network. For every topic, ask what it would mean for that offer. When you meet a framework, learn its purpose and its limits, not only its list of parts. Write definitions in your own words, then compare them with the textbook.

Practise the calculations until they are automatic: percentage margin, market share, break-even quantity, simple customer lifetime value. Show the formula, the units and the answer. Read business news for examples, but keep the theory in view. For the marketing plan project, start early, collect evidence, state assumptions, and keep the plan consistent from objectives to budget.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often treat marketing as advertising alone. Advertising is one part of promotion, and promotion is one part of the mix.

Other frequent errors include:
Confusing a target market with a whole population.
Writing a positioning statement that could describe any competitor.
Quoting a statistic without a source or date.
Mixing up profit margin and mark-up.
Treating one country’s consumer law as if it applied everywhere.
Producing a marketing plan with objectives that the budget cannot fund.
Ignoring ethics and consumer protection until the final chapter.

keyPoints: Marketing starts with customer needs and value, not with selling an existing product.
The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion, supported by research and segmentation.
Degree length, awards and exemptions vary by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Learn the calculations, because market share, margins and break-even are examined in figures.
Apply every framework to one real offer to see what it means in practice.
Consumer law and ethics differ by country, so name the country when you cite a rule.

en.title: Marketing principles and the marketing environment
en.short: This summary covers marketing’s nature, needs and wants, exchange, orientation, the mix, and the environment.

sections.heading: What marketing is
sections.text: Marketing is the activity of creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have value for customers and society. Its scope includes goods, services, ideas, places and people, and it applies to businesses, charities and public bodies. Marketing is not only selling: selling tries to move goods already made, while marketing starts by understanding needs and then shapes the offer.

sections.heading: Needs, wants and exchange
sections.text: A need is a basic requirement such as food, safety or belonging. A want is the form that need takes, shaped by culture and personality: one person wants garri, another wants bread. When a want is backed by buying power it becomes demand. Exchange is the core idea: two parties give something of value and both expect to gain. It requires two parties, something each values, freedom to accept or reject, and communication. A market is the set of actual and potential buyers who share a need.

sections.heading: Orientations and the mix
sections.text: Firms may follow a production orientation (efficiency), a product orientation (quality), a selling orientation (persuasion) or a marketing orientation (customer needs first). The marketing orientation argues that satisfied customers bring repeat sales and profit. The marketing mix is the set of controllable tools used to serve a target market. The 4Ps are product, price, place and promotion. Service firms often add people, process and physical evidence, making 7Ps. The mix must be consistent: a premium price needs a product and place that support it.

sections.heading: Environment and change
sections.text: The micro environment is close to the firm: the firm itself, customers, competitors, suppliers, intermediaries and publics (interested groups). The macro environment is wider and usually scanned with PESTLE: political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces. Environmental scanning means collecting and interpreting information about these forces to spot opportunities and threats. A made-up case: Ada sells spices in Lagos. She notices rising health interest and a new supermarket chain. She scans, then adjusts the mix: a low-salt range, new packs, supermarket listing, labelling and a fair price.

keyPoints: Marketing creates, communicates and delivers value; it is broader than selling or advertising.
A need is basic; a want is a culturally shaped form of it; demand is a want backed by buying power.
Exchange requires two parties, something of value, freedom to accept or reject, and communication.
A marketing orientation puts customer needs before production, product or selling goals.
The 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion) are controllable tools; services often add people, process and physical evidence.
Scanning the micro and macro environment helps a firm adjust its mix to change.

en.title: Consumer behaviour foundations
en.short: The buying decision process, influences, involvement, post-purchase behaviour and basic choice models.

sections.heading: The buying process
sections.text:
Consumer behaviour studies how people choose, buy, use and dispose of products. The common buying decision process has five stages: need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase, and post-purchase behaviour. The stages are a guide, not a fixed route. A routine purchase may skip search, while a costly one may loop back after new information.

Involvement is the personal importance and perceived risk of a purchase. It shapes how much effort a buyer gives to each stage.

sections.heading: Psychological and social influences
sections.text:
Psychological influences include motivation, perception, learning, beliefs and attitudes. Motivation is the drive to satisfy a need. Perception is how people select and interpret information. Learning changes behaviour through experience. Beliefs and attitudes guide evaluation.

Social influences include family, reference groups, roles and status. A reference group is any group a person compares with or looks to for guidance. Cultural influences include culture, subcultures and social class. Culture is shared values and customs learned in a society. These influences differ across countries, so check local meaning.

sections.heading: High and low involvement
sections.text:
High involvement purchases are expensive, risky or personally important. Buyers search more, compare attributes and feel post-purchase doubt, called cognitive dissonance. Low involvement purchases are frequent and low risk. Buyers rely on habit, price or a familiar cue.

Amina in Kano, Nigeria, needs a smartphone for online classes. She reads reviews, asks two friends and compares battery life and price. Her salt purchase is different: she takes the same brand without search. The phone is high involvement; the salt is low involvement.

sections.heading: Models and after purchase
sections.text:
Basic models of consumer choice include the economic or rational model, cognitive problem-solving models such as the Engel, Kollat and Blackwell model, and social models. Buyers often consider an evoked set, the small set of brands they remember and trust.

After purchase, satisfaction depends on expectations versus perceived performance. Good outcomes bring repeat buying and word of mouth; bad outcomes bring complaints and switching.

keyPoints: The buying decision process usually runs from need recognition to post-purchase behaviour, but stages can be skipped or repeated.
Psychological influences include motivation, perception, learning, beliefs and attitudes.
Social and cultural influences include family, reference groups, roles, culture, subcultures and social class.
High involvement purchases involve more search and post-purchase doubt; low involvement purchases rely on habit and simple cues.
Satisfaction after purchase depends on expectations compared with perceived performance.
Basic consumer choice models include economic, cognitive and social views, and buyers often choose from an evoked set.

en.title: Marketing information and the research process
en.short: How marketers turn information into decisions, from problem definition to ethical data collection.

sections.heading: The information system
sections.text: A marketing information system (MIS) is the people, equipment and procedures a firm uses to gather, sort, analyse and distribute information to marketing decision makers. It draws on internal records such as sales and customer databases, marketing intelligence such as competitor reports, and marketing research, which is project-based study of a specific marketing problem. A good MIS gives the right information at the right time, not simply more data. It helps managers see problems before they become crises.

sections.heading: Defining the problem
sections.text: Problem definition states the decision the manager faces and the information needed. It turns a broad concern into specific research objectives. For example, Ada’s Foods, a made-up snack company in Lagos, finds that repeat purchases are falling. The broad problem is falling loyalty. A useful objective is: find out why urban customers who bought twice do not buy again. A vague objective such as study customers wastes money.

sections.heading: Secondary and primary data
sections.text: Secondary data already exist, having been collected for another purpose. They include company sales records, government statistics, trade reports and academic articles. They are usually cheaper and faster, but may be outdated, incomplete or collected for a different question. Primary data are collected for the current problem through surveys, interviews, observation or experiments. They fit the question better but cost more time and money. Ada’s Foods might first read its loyalty records and industry reports, then interview a small sample of lapsed customers.

sections.heading: Research steps and ethics
sections.text: The research process usually follows these steps: define the problem and objectives; design the research plan, including data sources, methods, sampling (choosing who to study) and questionnaires; collect the data; analyse it; and present findings that support a decision. Ethics apply at every step. Participants should give informed consent, know the purpose, and be free to stop. Researchers must protect confidentiality and personal data, avoid harm and deception, and report results honestly. Data protection rules differ by country, so check the current local law.

keyPoints: A marketing information system supplies timely, accurate information from internal records, intelligence and research.
Problem definition turns a management decision into clear research objectives.
Secondary data are cheaper and faster but may not fit the current problem.
Primary data are collected for the specific problem and give better fit at higher cost.
The research process runs from problem definition through design, collection, analysis and reporting.
Ethical research requires informed consent, confidentiality, no harm and honest reporting.

en.title: Segmentation, targeting and positioning
en.short: How to divide markets, choose target segments, position offers and state a value proposition.

sections.heading: Segmenting markets
sections.text: Market segmentation divides a market into groups of buyers with similar needs or behaviour. Members of a segment should respond similarly to an offer. Consumer markets are segmented by geography, demographics such as age or income, psychographics such as lifestyle, and behaviour such as usage or loyalty. Business markets use firmographics: industry, size and location. They also use buying process, purchasing criteria and benefits sought, because a hospital and a small shop may buy the same product for different reasons.

sections.heading: Viable segments and targeting
sections.text: A viable segment meets five tests: measurable, substantial enough to serve profitably, accessible through available channels, differentiable from other segments, and actionable with the firm’s resources. Targeting means choosing which segments to serve. An undifferentiated strategy treats the whole market alike. A differentiated strategy serves several segments with separate offers. A concentrated or niche strategy serves one segment deeply. Micromarketing tailors offers to individuals or local groups. Choice depends on resources, competition and capabilities.

sections.heading: Positioning and value proposition
sections.text: Positioning is the place an offer occupies in the target customer’s mind relative to competitors. A positioning map, also called a perceptual map, plots brands on two attributes customers care about, such as price and convenience. It should use customer research, not only managers’ views. The value proposition is the bundle of benefits and price the firm promises. It is chosen after the target segment is known, and it must be true and distinctive. It is communicated through every touchpoint: product, pack, price, staff, advertising and proof.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Ada Foods in Enugu makes tomato paste. Research finds two groups: busy small households that value quick cooking, and large families that value low cost per gram. Ada targets the first group with a concentrated strategy. On a map with price on one axis and convenience on the other, its brand sits at high convenience and mid price. Its value proposition is quick, consistent paste for busy cooks at a fair price. Ada communicates this through easy-open packs, recipe adverts and shop demonstrations.

keyPoints: Segmentation groups buyers by similar needs; targeting chooses which groups to serve.
Consumer bases include geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural; business bases include firmographics and buying behaviour.
Viable segments should be measurable, substantial, accessible, differentiable and actionable.
Targeting can be undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated or micromarketing.
A positioning map shows customer perceptions on two chosen attributes.
The value proposition states the benefits and price promised, and must be proved at every touchpoint.

en.title: Product and brand basics
en.short: Product levels, consumer and industrial goods, product mix and basic branding choices.

sections.heading: Product levels
sections.text:
A product is anything offered to satisfy a need or want. Textbooks often describe three levels. The core product is the benefit the buyer seeks. The actual product is the good or service with its features, design, quality, packaging and brand name. The augmented product adds services such as delivery, installation, warranty or after-sales support. Some books add expected and potential levels.

Example: Amina’s Bakery in Kano sells bread. The core benefit is a fresh family meal. The actual product is the loaf, recipe, wrapping and name. The augmented product is home delivery and a freshness promise.

sections.heading: Classifying products
sections.text:
Consumer products are bought for personal or household use. Convenience products are bought often with little effort, such as bread or soap. Shopping products are compared on price and quality, such as furniture. Specialty products have a strong preference, such as a named artist’s work. Unsought products are not normally sought, such as insurance.

Industrial products are bought for business use. They include materials and parts, such as raw materials and components; capital items, such as machines and buildings; and supplies and services, such as lubricants and maintenance. The same item can fall in either class depending on the buyer and use.

sections.heading: Product mix and brand
sections.text:
The product mix is the set of items a firm sells. Managers decide its width (number of product lines), length (total items), depth (variants in a line) and consistency (how closely lines relate).

A brand is a name, term, sign, symbol, design or combination that identifies a seller’s goods and separates them from rivals. A brand name is the part that can be spoken. A logo is a visual symbol. An own label (private label or store brand) is owned by a retailer, not a manufacturer. Amina’s Bakery might use one family brand for bread and cakes, or separate names for each line. It should choose a name that is easy to say, lawful to protect and suitable for its market.

keyPoints: Product planners distinguish the core benefit, the actual product and the augmented product.
Consumer products are classified as convenience, shopping, specialty or unsought.
Industrial products include materials and parts, capital items, and supplies and services.
Product mix width, length, depth and consistency describe the range a firm sells.
A brand identifies a seller’s goods and separates them from competitors.
Branding choices include the brand name, the logo and whether to use a manufacturer brand or an own label.

en.title: Pricing fundamentals
en.short: Demand, elasticity, costs, competition, pricing objectives and three pricing methods.

sections.heading: Demand and elasticity
sections.text: Price elasticity of demand measures how quantity demanded responds to a change in price. It is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Demand is elastic when the absolute value is above 1, and inelastic when it is below 1. A price rise reduces total revenue when demand is elastic. It can raise revenue when demand is inelastic. Goods with close substitutes tend to be elastic; necessities tend to be inelastic.

sections.heading: Costs, competition and objectives
sections.text: Costs set a floor for price in the long run. Competition and customer value set a ceiling. Pricing objectives guide the choice: survival, profit, sales growth, market share, quality leadership or holding the current price. A firm may price low to enter a market or high to signal quality. Competitors’ prices and likely reactions matter, especially when few sellers dominate.

sections.heading: Three pricing methods
sections.text: Cost-plus pricing adds a standard markup to unit cost: price = unit cost × (1 + markup). Unit cost is variable cost plus fixed cost per expected unit. Target-return pricing sets price to earn a desired return on investment: price = (total cost + target profit) ÷ expected units. Value-based pricing starts from the customer’s perceived value and works back to cost. It can charge more when the offer saves time or money, but it needs evidence of that value.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up firm has variable cost 40 per unit, fixed cost 60,000 and expected sales of 5,000 units. Unit cost = 40 + 60,000 ÷ 5,000 = 52. With a 25% markup, cost-plus price = 52 × 1.25 = 65. For target return, investment is 200,000 and the target is 10%, so target profit = 20,000. Total cost = 40 × 5,000 + 60,000 = 260,000. Price = (260,000 + 20,000) ÷ 5,000 = 56. Check: profit = 56 × 5,000 − 260,000 = 20,000, which is 10% of 200,000.

keyPoints: Price elasticity of demand = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.
Demand is elastic when the absolute elasticity is above 1, and a price rise then reduces total revenue.
Costs set a floor and competition and customer value set a ceiling for price.
Cost-plus price = unit cost × (1 + markup).
Target-return price = (total cost + target profit) ÷ expected units.
Value-based pricing starts from perceived customer value rather than from cost.

en.title: Distribution channels and retailing
en.short: Channel functions, intermediaries, levels, wholesalers, retailers, formats and physical distribution.

sections.heading: Channel functions and levels
sections.text: A distribution channel is the set of organisations that move a product from producer to final user. Intermediaries are firms in between. They buy and sell, bear risk, store goods, break bulk, transport, finance and provide market information. By specialising, they reduce the number of contacts needed and create place, time and possession utility. A channel level counts the intermediaries between producer and consumer. Zero-level is direct selling. One-level is producer to retailer to consumer. Two-level adds a wholesaler. Three-level adds an agent. Business markets often use distributors and agents.

sections.heading: Wholesalers, retailers and formats
sections.text: Wholesalers buy in bulk and sell mainly to retailers, other wholesalers or business users. They break bulk (split large loads into smaller lots), hold stock, deliver, give trade credit (time to pay) and share market information. Retailers sell to final consumers and provide assortment (a range of goods), convenient location, opening hours, advice and after-sales service. Common store formats include independent shops, chain stores, supermarkets, hypermarkets, convenience stores, discount stores, department stores and speciality stores. Markets, kiosks and street traders matter in many countries. Non-store retailing includes e-commerce, direct selling and vending machines. In a made-up case, Ngozi runs a small shop in Enugu. She buys cartons of milk from a wholesaler, who buys from a distributor. The wholesaler stores stock and offers short credit; Ngozi sells single sachets near homes. Buying direct would tie up more of her capital and space.

sections.heading: Physical distribution
sections.text: Physical distribution, also called logistics, covers order processing, warehousing, inventory control, transport and materials handling. Its aim is to meet the service level customers expect at the lowest total cost. Managers trade off speed against cost: faster delivery and more stock raise cost, while slow delivery and stockouts (running out of stock) lose sales. Goods may move by road, rail, sea or air. The choice depends on weight, distance, urgency and infrastructure. Road transport is often used for last-mile delivery, especially where rail and port links are weak.

keyPoints: A distribution channel moves goods from producer to final user and may be direct or use intermediaries.
Intermediaries perform functions such as breaking bulk, storage, transport, financing and market information.
Channel level counts intermediaries; zero-level is direct, one-level uses a retailer, two-level adds a wholesaler.
Wholesalers sell mainly to retailers and business users; retailers sell to final consumers.
Retail formats differ by range, price, service and location, and include store and non-store types.
Physical distribution balances the service level customers expect against total logistics cost.

en.title: Promotion and integrated marketing communication basics
en.short: The communication process, promotion mix tools, push and pull, and planning integrated communication.

sections.heading: How communication works
sections.text: Promotion is communication. The sender encodes a message into words, images or symbols. The message travels through a channel, such as television, radio, print, a website or a salesperson. The receiver decodes it. Noise is anything that disturbs the message, such as a weak signal, a competing advert or a language gap. Feedback shows whether the message was received as intended. A marketer plans all these elements, not only the words.

sections.heading: The promotion mix
sections.text: The promotion mix is the set of tools a firm uses. Advertising is paid, non-personal communication with an identified sponsor. Sales promotion offers a short-term incentive, such as a discount, coupon or competition. Public relations builds goodwill through publicity, events and community work. Personal selling is face-to-face or direct conversation with a buyer. Direct and digital marketing uses mail, email, social media or search to invite a response. Each tool has different reach, cost and credibility.

sections.heading: Push and pull
sections.text: A push strategy directs promotion to channel members, such as wholesalers and retailers, to encourage them to stock and sell the product. A pull strategy directs promotion to final consumers, who then ask retailers for the product, pulling it through the channel. Many firms use both. A made-up soap maker may offer retailers a trade discount (push) and run consumer advertising (pull).

sections.heading: Planning and IMC
sections.text: Integrated marketing communication (IMC) means coordinating every promotional tool and message so they support one clear position. Basic planning follows steps: define the target audience, set measurable objectives, decide the budget, choose the mix, design the message, select media, set timing and measure results. A made-up bakery has ₦120,000 for promotion. It allocates 40% to advertising, 25% to sales promotion, 20% to public relations and 15% to personal selling. The amounts are ₦48,000, ₦30,000, ₦24,000 and ₦18,000. Check: 48,000 + 30,000 + 24,000 + 18,000 = ₦120,000. The split is a management choice, not a fixed rule.

keyPoints: Promotion is communication and must pass from sender to receiver with feedback.
The promotion mix includes advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling and direct or digital marketing.
Push promotes to channel members; pull promotes to final consumers.
IMC coordinates all messages around one clear position.
Plan by audience, objectives, budget, mix, message, media, timing and measurement.
Budget for a tool = total promotion budget × its share.

en.title: Marketing arithmetic and basic metrics
en.short: Market share, sales growth, margins, mark-up, break-even and return on marketing investment.

sections.heading: Core formulas
sections.text: Market share is a firm’s sales divided by total market sales, shown as a percentage. Sales growth compares two periods: (current sales − previous sales) ÷ previous sales × 100. Gross margin is (revenue − cost of goods sold) ÷ revenue × 100. Mark-up is (price − cost) ÷ cost × 100, so it is always higher than the margin on the same sale. Break-even volume is fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit, where contribution is price minus variable cost per unit. Return on marketing investment (ROMI) is (incremental contribution − campaign cost) ÷ campaign cost × 100.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Ada sells juice. Last year revenue was ₦4,000,000; this year it is ₦5,000,000. Total market sales are ₦50,000,000. Cost of goods sold is ₦3,000,000. Fixed costs are ₦600,000. Price per bottle is ₦500 and variable cost is ₦300.
Market share = 5,000,000 ÷ 50,000,000 = 10%.
Sales growth = (5,000,000 − 4,000,000) ÷ 4,000,000 = 25%.
Gross margin = (5,000,000 − 3,000,000) ÷ 5,000,000 = 40%.
Mark-up = (500 − 300) ÷ 300 = 66.7%.
Contribution per bottle = 500 − 300 = ₦200.
Break-even volume = 600,000 ÷ 200 = 3,000 bottles.
A campaign costs ₦200,000 and adds 1,500 bottles of sales. Extra contribution = 1,500 × 200 = ₦300,000. Net gain = 300,000 − 200,000 = ₦100,000.
ROMI = 100,000 ÷ 200,000 = 50%.

sections.heading: Using the figures
sections.text: Market share shows position against rivals, but check whether the market is defined widely or narrowly. Sales growth of 25% is good only if the market grew more slowly; if the market grew 30%, share fell. Gross margin and mark-up describe the same sale from different bases: a 40% margin equals a 66.7% mark-up. Break-even says Ada must sell 3,000 bottles to cover fixed costs; each extra bottle adds ₦200 contribution. A ROMI of 50% means each ₦1 of campaign spend returned ₦1.50 in extra contribution, leaving ₦0.50 net. Use these figures to compare options, not as proof of cause.

keyPoints: Market share = firm sales ÷ total market sales × 100.
Sales growth = (current sales − previous sales) ÷ previous sales × 100.
Gross margin = (revenue − cost of goods sold) ÷ revenue × 100; mark-up = (price − cost) ÷ cost × 100.
Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit, where contribution = price − variable cost per unit.
ROMI = (incremental contribution − campaign cost) ÷ campaign cost × 100.
A high mark-up can sit beside a modest margin, so state which base you are using.

en.title: Marketing research: design and analysis
en.short: Research designs, sampling, sample size, questionnaires, interviews, focus groups and basic analysis.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text: Research design is the plan for collecting and analysing evidence. Exploratory research clarifies a problem, descriptive research measures it, and causal research tests cause and effect, often by experiment. Sampling chooses part of a population to represent the whole. Probability methods, such as simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster sampling, give every member a known chance of selection. Non-probability methods, such as convenience, quota and purposive sampling, are quicker but cannot support strict statistical generalisation.

sections.heading: Sample size and questionnaires
sections.text:
Sample size depends on confidence level, margin of error, variability and the smallest subgroup you must report. For a proportion, n = z² p(1−p) ÷ e².
At 95% confidence z = 1.96; with p = 0.5 and e = 0.05:
n = 1.96² × 0.25 ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so 385.
Questionnaire design means clear, neutral questions in a sensible order. Avoid leading, double-barrelled and ambiguous items, use screening questions, and pre-test on a small group. Likert scales are common but must be labelled.

sections.heading: Interviews and focus groups
sections.text: Qualitative interviews explore beliefs and experiences in depth. They may be structured, semi-structured or unstructured; semi-structured is common in marketing. Focus groups bring six to ten people together to discuss a topic, guided by a moderator. They show shared language and disagreement, but group pressure can silence views. Record with consent, transcribe, and analyse by coding and grouping into themes. Qualitative work answers why and how, not how many.

sections.heading: Worked analysis
sections.text:
A made-up survey of 200 shoppers finds 120 prefer a new pack. Preference is 120 ÷ 200 = 60%.
The standard error is √(0.6 × 0.4 ÷ 200) = 0.0346, so an approximate 95% confidence interval is 0.6 ± 1.96 × 0.0346, from 53.2% to 66.8%.
If a previous survey found 50% preference, the difference is 10 percentage points. Cross-tabulation compares answers by segment, for example 70% of younger shoppers against 52% of older shoppers. Report bases and avoid over-reading small differences. Set the decision rule before analysis.

keyPoints: Exploratory, descriptive and causal designs answer different questions.
Probability sampling supports statistical generalisation; non-probability sampling does not.
For a proportion, n = z² p(1−p) ÷ e²; for a finite population N, adjust with n ÷ (1 + (n − 1) ÷ N).
Questionnaires must avoid leading, double-barrelled and ambiguous questions, and be pre-tested.
Focus groups reveal shared views but group pressure can distort them.
A 95% confidence interval for a proportion is p ± 1.96 × √(p(1−p) ÷ n).

en.title: Services marketing
en.short: Service characteristics, quality and gaps models, servicescape, demand and capacity, and recovery.

sections.heading: What makes a service
sections.text: Services are acts or performances, not things. Four characteristics are usually taught. Intangibility means a service cannot be seen or touched before purchase, so customers rely on cues such as staff and reputation. Inseparability means production and consumption often happen together, and the customer takes part. Variability means each delivery can differ. Perishability means unused capacity is lost, such as an empty seat on a flight. Goods can be stored and resold; services cannot. Marketing shifts toward managing people, process and physical evidence.

sections.heading: Quality and gaps
sections.text: Service quality is the customer’s judgement of delivery against expectations. SERVQUAL, from Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry, measures five dimensions: reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles. Reliability, doing what was promised, is usually most important. Grönroos separates technical quality (what is received) from functional quality (how). The gaps model locates failure between expectations and management understanding, service specifications, delivery, and external communication. A promised same-day delivery that operations cannot meet creates a gap. Closing gaps needs research, clear standards, trained staff and honest promotion.

sections.heading: Place and capacity
sections.text: The servicescape is the physical environment where the service happens: layout, lighting, sound, signs and cleanliness. It shapes mood and expectations. Demand and capacity are managed by smoothing demand with reservations, appointments and off-peak pricing, by adjusting capacity with part-time staff and extended hours, and by managing waits with queuing. A restaurant has 40 seats and turns each seat three times in an evening, so capacity is 40 × 3 = 120 covers (diners served). If demand is 150, 30 customers wait or are lost.

sections.heading: Service recovery
sections.text: Service recovery is what a firm does after failure. Effective recovery is quick, fair and empathetic, and it fixes the cause. Staff need authority to resolve complaints. Recovery cannot replace reliable service. Example: Ada books a hotel room in Abuja; it is double-booked. The hotel apologises, finds equivalent accommodation, pays the transfer and gives a free night. The cost is small against losing her future bookings.

keyPoints: Services are intangible, inseparable, variable and perishable, so they cannot be stored like goods.
SERVQUAL measures reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles.
The gaps model traces service failure to gaps in understanding, standards, delivery and communication.
The servicescape is the physical setting that shapes customer expectations and behaviour.
Capacity = seats × turns; compare it with demand to plan queues or reservations.
Service recovery should be quick, fair and root-cause focused, not just an apology.

en.title: Brand management and brand equity
en.short: Brand equity, positioning, architecture, extensions, measurement and portfolio management.

sections.heading: Brand equity
sections.text: Brand equity is the extra value a brand name adds to a product. In customer-based brand equity, as Keller describes it, the brand creates a different customer response than an unbranded version. It comes from awareness, strong associations, perceived quality and loyalty. Aaker adds assets such as trademarks and channel relationships. High equity can support higher prices, repeat purchase and bargaining power.

sections.heading: Positioning and architecture
sections.text: Brand positioning is the place a brand occupies in the customer’s mind relative to competitors. It uses points of difference, which customers value and competitors lack, and points of parity, which are necessary. A perceptual map plots brands on two attributes. Brand architecture is how a firm organises its brands. A branded house uses one main name, such as Virgin. A house of brands keeps separate names, such as Unilever. Endorsed and hybrid structures sit between.

sections.heading: Extensions and measurement
sections.text: Brand extension uses an existing brand name in a new category. Success depends on category fit, parent brand strength and consumer trust. Poor fit can dilute the brand. Measurement uses customer surveys for awareness, associations and loyalty, market data for share and price premium, and financial brand valuation. A branded bag sells for 1,200 naira and an identical unbranded bag for 1,000 naira. If the branded bag sells 50,000 units, the total price premium is 200 × 50,000 = 10,000,000 naira. This is one sign, not total equity.

sections.heading: Portfolio management
sections.text: A brand portfolio is the set of brands a firm owns. Managers give each brand a role: cash cow, fighter brand, entry-level brand or prestige brand. They avoid overlap that causes cannibalisation, where one brand steals sales from another. They allocate resources and prune weak brands. For example, Zuri Foods owns Zuri Gold for premium buyers and Zuri Everyday for value buyers. Clear roles reduce internal competition and help each brand serve a distinct segment.

keyPoints: Brand equity is the extra value a brand name adds beyond the functional product.
Customer-based brand equity rests on awareness, associations, perceived quality and loyalty.
Positioning uses points of difference and points of parity; a perceptual map shows relative positions.
Brand architecture ranges from a branded house to a house of brands, with endorsed and hybrid forms between.
Brand extensions need category fit and a strong parent brand; poor fit can dilute equity.
Total price premium = (branded price − unbranded price) × branded units sold, and portfolios need clear roles to avoid cannibalisation.

en.title: Business-to-business marketing
en.short: Organisational buying, buying centres, derived demand, B2B segmentation, value propositions, channels and pricing.

sections.heading: Organisational buying
sections.text:
Business-to-business (B2B) marketing sells goods and services to organisations that use them to produce other goods, run operations or resell. Organisational buying behaviour is often more formal and longer than consumer buying. A buying centre is the group that takes part in a purchase. Its roles include users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers, who control access to information. One person may hold several roles.

Demand is derived: a packaging supplier’s sales depend on demand for the food inside the pack. A fall in consumer demand soon reduces orders for machinery, materials and transport. This makes B2B demand volatile and sensitive to customers’ forecasts.

sections.heading: Segmentation and value
sections.text:
B2B segmentation groups customers by needs and by observable traits. Firmographics include industry, size, location and ownership. Buyers also differ in purchasing policy, order size, technical requirements and risk. A supplier may target, say, mid-sized food processors in Nigeria that need reliable cold-chain delivery.

The value proposition should speak to the buying centre, not only the user. It may promise lower total cost of ownership, fewer breakdowns, compliance support or faster delivery. Total cost of ownership adds purchase price to installation, energy, maintenance, downtime and disposal. A higher price can still win if it reduces these costs.

sections.heading: Channels and pricing
sections.text:
B2B channels are often shorter and more direct. Large orders may go through a manufacturer’s own sales force or a systems integrator; smaller ones may use distributors. Fewer intermediaries mean the seller must provide technical advice, installation and after-sales support.

Pricing differs from consumer markets. B2B prices are frequently negotiated for each contract or set by competitive tender. Sellers use list prices with volume discounts, cost-plus contracts or value-based prices tied to customer savings. Payment terms, leasing and service contracts matter as much as the headline price.

Case: Ada Foods in Enugu wants a new filling line. Production, finance and quality staff form the buying centre. The supplier’s proposal stresses payback from less waste, not a low sticker price.

keyPoints: B2B marketing serves organisations whose demand is derived from consumer demand.
The buying centre includes users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers.
B2B segmentation combines firmographics with purchasing needs and behaviour.
A strong value proposition addresses total cost of ownership and risk for the whole buying centre.
B2B channels tend to be shorter and more direct, with more technical support.
B2B prices are often negotiated or tendered rather than set as fixed consumer prices.

en.title: Digital marketing and social media
en.short: Digital channels, search, content, social, email, mobile, the customer journey, analytics and campaign planning.

sections.heading: Channels and journey
sections.text: Digital marketing uses online channels to reach and serve customers. Channels include search, content, social media, email and mobile. They can be paid, owned or earned. Paid media buys reach; owned media are controlled assets such as websites; earned media are shares and mentions. The digital customer journey has stages: awareness, consideration, conversion, retention and advocacy. Customers often move across touchpoints in no fixed order. Attribution gives credit to touchpoints, but it is imperfect.

sections.heading: Search and content
sections.text: Search engine optimisation (SEO) improves unpaid ranking through relevant content, technical access and links. Paid search, often called search engine marketing (SEM), buys ads on pay-per-click (PPC) terms: the advertiser pays when a user clicks. Content marketing creates and shares useful material to attract and keep an audience. It should match search intent and the journey stage.

sections.heading: Social, email and mobile
sections.text: Social media marketing uses platforms to build reach, community and dialogue. Organic posts earn attention; paid social buys targeting. Email marketing sends permission-based messages to a list. Segmentation and personalisation raise relevance, and consent is essential. Mobile marketing uses SMS, apps and mobile web. It offers immediacy and location, but must respect privacy and local law.

sections.heading: Analytics and planning
sections.text:
Basic digital analytics measures behaviour. Click-through rate (CTR) = clicks ÷ impressions. Conversion rate = conversions ÷ clicks. Cost per click (CPC) = spend ÷ clicks. Cost per acquisition (CPA) = spend ÷ conversions. Return on ad spend (ROAS) = revenue ÷ spend.

Example: 100,000 impressions, 2% CTR gives 2,000 clicks. Spend 40,000 gives CPC 20. At 5% conversion, 100 conversions, CPA 400. Revenue of 1,000 per conversion is 100,000, so ROAS is 2.5.

Campaign planning sets objectives, audience, channels, budget, content, schedule and measurement. Test small, then scale. Attribution and testing improve decisions.

keyPoints: Digital channels are paid, owned or earned, and the customer journey is not a straight line.
SEO earns unpaid search visibility; PPC buys clicks.
Email and mobile marketing require consent and respect local data protection law.
CTR = clicks ÷ impressions; conversion rate = conversions ÷ clicks.
CPA = spend ÷ conversions; ROAS = revenue ÷ spend.
Plan campaigns with clear objectives, audience, budget, content and measurement, and test before scaling.

en.title: Sales management and personal selling
en.short: Organising, staffing, motivating and evaluating a sales force, plus the selling process and forecasts.

sections.heading: Organising the sales force
sections.text: Sales management plans, directs and controls personal selling: direct communication with a buyer to create value and close a sale. A sales force may be organised by geography, product, customer type or a combination. Territory design divides accounts into areas. A good territory balances sales potential and workload, travel time and coverage. In a simple workload check, 600 accounts called on eight times a year need 4,800 calls. If one salesperson can make 1,200 calls a year, the firm needs 4,800 ÷ 1,200 = 4 salespeople.

sections.heading: Recruitment, training and pay
sections.text: Recruitment starts with a job description and person specification, then uses internal or external sources. Training covers products, customers, selling skills, systems and ethics. Motivation and compensation must fit the selling job. A salary gives security; commission links pay to sales; a bonus rewards targets or margins. Most firms use a mix. Commission can encourage pressure selling or neglect of after-sales work, so managers add service and profit measures. Coaching, recognition and fair quotas also motivate.

sections.heading: The selling process
sections.text: The usual steps are prospecting, qualifying, pre-approach, approach, presentation, handling objections, closing and follow-up. Prospecting finds possible buyers; qualifying checks need, authority and ability to pay. Pre-approach prepares information. The presentation matches benefits to needs. Objections are answered with evidence, not argument. Closing asks for a decision. Follow-up confirms delivery and builds repeat business.

sections.heading: Forecasting and evaluation
sections.text: A sales forecast estimates future sales. Qualitative methods include the sales force composite, executive opinion and the Delphi method. Quantitative methods include moving averages, regression and weighted pipeline. In a weighted pipeline, each opportunity is multiplied by its probability. Three deals worth 40,000, 60,000 and 100,000 at 50%, 25% and 10% give (40,000 × 0.50) + (60,000 × 0.25) + (100,000 × 0.10) = 20,000 + 15,000 + 10,000 = 45,000. Evaluation compares actual sales with quotas or forecasts, and reviews call rates, conversion rates and cost per call. Variance = actual − target.

keyPoints: Sales forces can be organised by geography, product, customer or a combination.
Territory design balances sales potential and workload, including travel and coverage.
Recruitment uses a job description and person specification; training covers products, customers, selling skills, systems and ethics.
Compensation often mixes salary, commission and bonus; commission motivates sales but can distort behaviour.
The selling process runs from prospecting and qualifying through presentation, objections and closing to follow-up.
Weighted pipeline forecast = Σ (opportunity value × probability); variance = actual − target.

en.title: Advertising and campaign management
en.short: Objectives, creative and media plans, budgets, evaluation and regulation of advertising campaigns.

sections.heading: Objectives and creative strategy
sections.text:
Advertising objectives state what a campaign must achieve. They can be communication objectives, such as awareness, recall or attitude change, or sales objectives. Good objectives name the target audience, the change sought, the measure and the time limit. Hierarchy models such as AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action) are planning aids, not proof that buyers always move in steps.

Creative strategy is the plan for the message. It sets the target audience, the main proposition, supporting reasons, appeal, tone and execution style. It must fit the brand’s positioning and be tested before large spending.

sections.heading: Media planning and buying
sections.text:
Media planning chooses media and a schedule to reach the target audience. Reach is the number or percentage of different people exposed at least once. Frequency is the average number of exposures per person reached. Impressions are total exposures. CPM, cost per thousand impressions, is (cost ÷ impressions) × 1,000. Media buying is negotiating and buying space or time.

Example: a plan needs 1,000,000 impressions at a CPM of ₦2,500. Cost = (1,000,000 ÷ 1,000) × 2,500 = ₦2,500,000. A ₦2,000,000 budget buys (2,000,000 ÷ 2,500) × 1,000 = 800,000 impressions.

sections.heading: Budgeting and evaluation
sections.text: Budgets are set by percentage of sales, competitive parity, what the firm can afford, or the objective-and-task method. Objective-and-task is usually preferred because it costs out the work needed to meet stated objectives. Evaluation uses pre-testing, such as copy tests, and post-testing, such as recall surveys, brand tracking and sales lift against a control group. Compare results with the objectives, not just with last year.

sections.heading: Regulation varies
sections.text: Advertising regulation varies by country. Common principles are that ads must be legal, decent, honest and truthful, with extra rules for children, health claims, alcohol and financial products. Nigeria’s Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON) regulates advertising there. The UK’s Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and South Africa’s Advertising Regulatory Board (ARB) play comparable roles. Check the current local code.

keyPoints: Advertising objectives should name the target, the desired response, the measure and the time limit.
Creative strategy sets the proposition, appeal, tone and execution, and should be tested before big spending.
Reach counts different people exposed; frequency counts average exposures per person reached.
CPM = (cost ÷ impressions) × 1,000, and impressions = (budget ÷ CPM) × 1,000.
Objective-and-task budgeting links spending to objectives; evaluate with pre-tests and post-tests against those objectives.
Advertising rules differ by country; check the current local code and the relevant regulator.

en.title: Marketing strategy and planning
en.short: Strategic marketing, portfolio analysis, Ansoff growth options, competitive positioning, planning and control.

sections.heading: Strategic marketing
sections.text: Strategic marketing is the long-term process of choosing which markets and customers to serve and how to build a defensible advantage. It differs from day-to-day marketing management because it asks where the organisation should compete, not only how to sell today. A strategic business unit (SBU) is a part of a firm with its own market and strategy. Strategy must fit the firm’s resources and the external environment.

sections.heading: Portfolio and growth
sections.text: Portfolio analysis reviews SBUs or products as a set. The BCG growth-share matrix classifies them by market growth and relative market share. Stars have high growth and high share; cash cows have low growth and high share; question marks have high growth and low share; dogs have low growth and low share. Relative share = own share ÷ largest rival’s share. If own share is 30% and the rival has 60%, relative share is 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5. The Ansoff matrix sets growth options: market penetration, market development, product development and diversification.

sections.heading: Competitive positioning
sections.text: Competitive positioning is the place a brand occupies in customers’ minds compared with rivals. It rests on a clear value proposition and on choices about price, quality, service and image. Michael Porter’s generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and focus. A firm must avoid being stuck in the middle, though later writers debate how strict this is. Positioning must be supported by real capabilities, not slogans.

sections.heading: Planning and control
sections.text: The marketing planning process moves from situation analysis to objectives, strategy, tactics, budget, implementation and control. Objectives should be specific and measurable. Marketing control compares actual results with the plan and corrects gaps. Annual plan control checks sales, share and expenses; profitability control examines profit by product, customer or channel; efficiency control reviews spending; strategic control uses a marketing audit to check whether the strategy still fits. A made-up firm, Nia Foods in Lagos, reviews its lines each year and shifts budget from a dog to a question mark only after testing demand.

keyPoints: Strategic marketing decides where to compete and how to build sustainable advantage.
Portfolio analysis reviews products or SBUs as a set, often with the BCG growth-share matrix.
Relative market share = own market share ÷ largest rival’s market share.
The Ansoff matrix gives four growth options: penetration, market development, product development and diversification.
Competitive positioning needs a clear value proposition; Porter’s generic strategies (cost leadership, differentiation and focus) describe how a firm competes.
Marketing control compares results with the plan and uses annual plan, profitability, efficiency and strategic controls.

en.title: International marketing
en.short: Global environment, entry modes, standardisation versus adaptation, branding, cross-border pricing and distribution.

sections.heading: Global environment
sections.text: International marketing means planning and carrying out marketing across national borders. The global marketing environment has economic, political and legal, cultural and technological parts. Income levels, exchange rates and inflation affect demand. Tariffs, product standards, labelling rules and ownership limits affect what a firm may do. Culture shapes language, colour, taste and negotiation style. These forces differ by country and change, so check current official sources such as customs and standards bodies.

sections.heading: Entry modes
sections.text: Firms choose entry modes by risk, control and speed. Exporting is selling from home, often through agents or distributors; it is low risk but gives less control. Licensing lets a foreign firm use intellectual property for a fee. Franchising adds a full business format. A joint venture shares ownership with a local partner. A wholly owned subsidiary gives most control but carries most risk. Contract manufacturing outsources production. Choice depends on the market, the product and the firm’s resources.

sections.heading: Standardise or adapt
sections.text: Standardisation uses one marketing mix worldwide to save costs and build a consistent image. Adaptation changes product, price, promotion or distribution for local needs. The debate is often called global integration versus local responsiveness. Most firms use glocalisation: standardise the core brand and adapt the execution. A soap may keep its name and formula but change scent, pack size and advertising. Adaptation can raise costs; standardisation can miss local tastes and rules.

sections.heading: Branding, pricing, distribution
sections.text: Global branding needs a name, legal checks and consistent positioning. Pricing across borders faces price escalation: transport, insurance, duty and intermediaries add to the export price. Distribution may use long channels, local partners and different retail structures. Incoterms, from the International Chamber of Commerce, set who pays freight and when risk passes. Example: a Ghanaian furniture maker sells FOB Tema for US$10,000. FOB (free on board) means the seller loads the goods on the ship at Tema and the buyer pays freight and insurance from there. The importer pays freight and insurance of US$1,500, so the CIF value (FOB plus freight plus insurance) is US$11,500. An illustrative 20% duty on the CIF value gives landed cost (10,000 + 1,500) × 1.20 = US$13,800. Check duty rates and the Incoterms edition.

keyPoints: International marketing adapts the marketing mix to different national environments.
Entry modes trade off control, risk and speed: exporting, licensing, franchising, joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries.
Standardisation lowers cost and builds consistency; adaptation meets local needs; glocalisation combines both.
Global brands need legal protection and consistent positioning across markets.
Price escalation comes from freight, insurance, duties and channel margins, so check each country’s rules.
Landed cost in the example = (FOB + freight + insurance) × (1 + duty rate) = (10,000 + 1,500) × 1.20 = US$13,800.

en.title: Marketing ethics and consumer protection
en.short: Ethical issues, CSR, vulnerable consumers and consumer protection law, with national rules to check.

sections.heading: Ethical issues
sections.text: Marketing ethics is the study of what marketers should do, not only what the law allows. A central test is whether a practice respects customers’ ability to make an informed choice. Common issues include deceptive claims, false urgency, high-pressure selling, misuse of personal data, targeting children or people in distress, bribery and products designed to fail early. Deceptive marketing creates a false impression even when each word is literally true. Ethical marketing requires truthfulness, fairness, transparency and respect for privacy.

sections.heading: Corporate social responsibility
sections.text: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is a firm’s voluntary commitment to consider stakeholders and society beyond its legal duties. Stakeholders include customers, employees, suppliers, communities and owners. CSR can mean safer products, honest labelling, fair sourcing and community projects. It builds trust only when it is genuine. Greenwashing is a CSR or environmental claim that sounds responsible but is not supported by evidence. CSR adds to the law; it never replaces a legal duty.

sections.heading: Vulnerable consumers and law
sections.text: Vulnerable consumers are people less able to understand information, exercise choice or complain. Age, disability, low literacy, language, poverty, illness or emotional distress can create vulnerability. Marketers should adjust claims, selling methods and complaint routes for them. Consumer protection law sets minimum rights, often covering safety, accurate information, unfair practices, cancellation rights, data protection and redress. Rules vary by country and change, so check the current national statute and regulator. Examples include Nigeria’s Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018, South Africa’s Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008 and the UK Consumer Rights Act 2015.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Case: Adaeze runs a pharmacy in Lagos. A supplier asks her to display posters saying a supplement 'cures diabetes in 14 days'. She has no reliable evidence. The claim could mislead older customers and delay care. Ethically she should refuse or ask for proof; legally she should check NAFDAC product registration and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission’s guidance. A CSR project funding health checks would not excuse the false claim.

keyPoints: Ethics asks what is right beyond the legal minimum.
Deceptive marketing can mislead even when every statement is literally true.
CSR is voluntary responsibility to stakeholders and society, and it does not replace legal duties.
Greenwashing is a responsible-sounding claim without evidence.
Vulnerable consumers need clearer information, fairer selling and easy complaint routes.
Consumer protection rules vary by country, so check the current national law and regulator.

en.title: Relationship marketing and customer relationship management
en.short: Building loyalty, measuring customer lifetime value, CRM systems, data privacy and customer experience.

sections.heading: From transactions to relationships
sections.text:
Relationship marketing aims to keep customers by building trust and commitment over many contacts, rather than winning a single sale. Morgan and Hunt argued in 1994 that trust and commitment are central to a successful relationship. The firm keeps its promises, communicates honestly and handles complaints well.

Loyalty is not the same as repeat buying. A customer may return out of habit, convenience or because switching is hard. True loyalty combines repeat purchase with a positive attitude, so it survives a competitor’s price cut.

sections.heading: Customer lifetime value
sections.text:
Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the profit a customer brings over the whole relationship, not just the first sale. It shows what is worth spending to keep them.

Example: a customer pays ₦20,000 a year and the firm keeps 30% as margin, so ₦6,000 a year. The average customer stays four years.
CLV = 6,000 × 4 = ₦24,000.
If winning that customer costs ₦15,000, net value is 24,000 − 15,000 = ₦9,000.
Discounting future profit would lower this figure; the simple version ignores it.

sections.heading: CRM systems and experience
sections.text:
Customer relationship management (CRM) is both a strategy and the software that supports it. Operational CRM handles daily contact: sales records, service tickets, call logs. Analytical CRM studies that data to segment customers and predict who may leave, called churn. Collaborative CRM shares information across sales, service and partners.

Customer experience is the sum of every touchpoint, from advert to complaint. Good CRM lets staff see the whole history, so service feels joined-up.

sections.heading: Data privacy
sections.text:
CRM runs on personal data, and the rules differ by country. The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies from 2018. Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 replaced earlier rules; South Africa’s POPIA and Kenya’s Data Protection Act 2019 cover their own territories. Most require a lawful basis such as consent, limits on use, security, and rights to access or delete data.

Rules change, so check the current text from the national regulator.

keyPoints: Relationship marketing seeks long-term relationships built on trust and commitment, not single sales.
Repeat purchase is not proof of loyalty; attitude matters too.
CLV = annual margin × expected years, before any discounting.
Compare CLV with the cost of winning the customer to judge net value.
CRM has operational, analytical and collaborative parts.
Data protection law differs by country, so check the national regulator.

en.title: Marketing analytics and performance measurement
en.short: Metrics, dashboards, A/B tests, attribution, ROMI and performance measurement.

sections.heading: Metrics and dashboards
sections.text: Marketing analytics turns data into decisions. A marketing metric is a number that tracks a marketing activity or result, such as conversion rate or cost per acquisition (CPA). A dashboard is a small set of linked metrics shown together, often weekly, so managers can see trends and act. Performance measurement compares actual results with targets, budgets and benchmarks, and asks whether marketing caused the change. Choose metrics that connect to a goal, define each one precisely and keep the same definition over time; otherwise comparisons mislead.

sections.heading: Experiments and A/B tests
sections.text: An experiment compares a treatment with a control. In an A/B test, random assignment sends users or customers to version A or version B. Randomisation makes the groups similar except for the change, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to that change. Decide the sample size and primary metric before starting. A result is statistically significant when it is unlikely to arise by chance alone; significance does not prove commercial importance.

sections.heading: Attribution and ROMI
sections.text: Attribution assigns credit for a sale or sign-up to touchpoints such as search, email or display. Last-click attribution gives all credit to the final touch; it is simple but undervalues earlier work. Multi-touch rules share credit. All attribution models are assumptions, so use them with experiments. Return on marketing investment (ROMI) compares incremental contribution with spend; one common formula is ROMI = (incremental contribution − marketing spend) ÷ marketing spend. A positive ROMI means the activity returned more contribution than it cost.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A campaign costs ₦200,000 and reaches 50,000 people. It produces 1,000 orders, so conversion rate = 1,000 ÷ 50,000 = 2%. Revenue is ₦600,000 and variable cost is ₦300,000, so contribution before marketing is ₦300,000. ROMI = (300,000 − 200,000) ÷ 200,000 = 0.5, or 50%. CPA = 200,000 ÷ 1,000 = ₦200. Check: 1,000 orders bring ₦300,000 contribution; after ₦200,000 spend, ₦100,000 remains.

keyPoints: Define each metric precisely and keep the definition stable for comparisons.
A dashboard should show a few linked metrics that support decisions, not every available number.
Random assignment in an A/B test lets you attribute outcome differences to the change.
Attribution models are assumptions; last-click undervalues earlier touchpoints.
ROMI = (incremental contribution − marketing spend) ÷ marketing spend, though definitions vary.
CPA = marketing spend ÷ number of acquisitions, and conversion rate = conversions ÷ audience.

en.title: Product development and innovation
en.short: NPD process, screening, business analysis, test marketing, launch, adoption and the product life cycle.

sections.heading: The development process
sections.text: The new product development (NPD) process moves an idea from concept to market. A common sequence is idea generation, screening, concept development and testing, marketing strategy, business analysis, product development, test marketing and commercialisation. A stage-gate process reviews each stage before the next, so weak ideas stop early. Idea generation draws on customers, staff, suppliers, competitors and research. Screening judges fit with strategy, skills and resources. A product concept describes the idea so customers can evaluate it.

sections.heading: Business analysis and testing
sections.text: Business analysis forecasts sales, costs, investment and profit before heavy spending. A made-up firm, Adeyemi Foods in Lagos, plans a snack with fixed launch costs of ₦12,000,000, price ₦1,500 and variable cost ₦900 a unit. Contribution per unit is ₦1,500 − ₦900 = ₦600. Break-even volume is ₦12,000,000 ÷ ₦600 = 20,000 units. At a forecast of 30,000 units, profit is (30,000 × ₦600) − ₦12,000,000 = ₦6,000,000. Test marketing sells in a limited area to measure trial, repeat purchase and complaints. Launch sets timing, place, promotion and price, often by regional rollout.

sections.heading: Adoption and diffusion
sections.text: Adoption is one customer’s decision to buy and use a new product. Diffusion is the spread of that product through a market over time. Everett Rogers described five adopter groups: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards. He also named five product attributes that affect speed: relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability. Products that are clearly better, easy to use, easy to try and visible spread faster. Word of mouth and opinion leaders matter.

sections.heading: Product life cycle
sections.text: The product life cycle (PLC) shows sales and profit patterns over four stages: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. In introduction, sales are low and promotion is heavy. Growth brings rising sales and new competitors. Maturity has stable sales, strong competition and price pressure. Decline follows falling demand. The PLC is a planning tool, not a law: some skip stages or stay mature for years. Firms may extend maturity by improving the product, finding new users or entering new markets.

keyPoints: The NPD process runs from idea generation and screening through business analysis, development, test marketing and launch.
Screening checks strategic fit and resources before money is committed.
Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit, and profit = (units × contribution per unit) − fixed costs.
Test marketing measures trial and repeat purchase in a limited market before a full launch.
Rogers’ diffusion model names five adopter groups and five product attributes that affect adoption speed.
The product life cycle has introduction, growth, maturity and decline stages, but it is a planning tool, not a fixed law.

en.title: Pricing strategy and tactics
en.short: Skimming, penetration, value and cost pricing, discrimination, psychology, discounts and competitive response.

sections.heading: Strategic price choices
sections.text:
Cost-based pricing starts from the firm’s costs. Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to unit cost. It is simple and covers costs, but ignores what customers will pay and what rivals charge. Value-based pricing starts from the customer’s perceived value and works back to a price and allowable cost. It needs evidence.

Skimming sets a high launch price to recover costs from early buyers, then lowers it. It suits innovative or prestige products with few substitutes. Penetration pricing sets a low price to win share, then may rise. It suits price-sensitive markets and products with scale economies, but can damage margins.

sections.heading: Discrimination and psychology
sections.text:
Price discrimination charges customers different prices for the same product. It works when segments differ in willingness to pay and resale is hard. Examples include student fares, off-peak travel and quantity discounts. It must respect competition and consumer law, which varies by country.

Psychological pricing uses how buyers interpret numbers. Odd pricing such as 1,999 may look lower than 2,000. Prestige pricing keeps a high price as a quality signal. Reference prices are standards buyers compare against. Discounts include cash, trade, quantity and seasonal discounts. Repeated discounts train customers to wait and weaken the brand.

sections.heading: Worked example and response
sections.text:
A firm has unit variable cost ₦4,000, fixed costs ₦2,000,000 and expects 1,000 units. Full unit cost = 4,000 + (2,000,000 ÷ 1,000) = ₦6,000. A 25% cost-plus markup gives 6,000 × 1.25 = ₦7,500. At 1,000 units, revenue is ₦7,500,000, total cost is ₦6,000,000 and profit is ₦1,500,000. If customers value it at ₦9,000, a value-based price of ₦8,500 may capture more value.

Competitive price response should follow the strategy. A firm should know whether a rival’s cut threatens a key segment or is temporary. It can respond with non-price tools such as service, bundling or communication, or match only where necessary. Matching everywhere can start a price war.

keyPoints: Cost-plus price = unit cost × (1 + markup).
Skimming sets a high launch price and lowers it later; penetration sets a low price to build share.
Value-based pricing begins with the customer’s perceived value, not with the firm’s costs.
Price discrimination needs separated segments, limited resale and compliance with the law of the country.
Psychological pricing and discounts change perceived value, but repeated discounts can train buyers to wait.
Competitive price response should be selective and may use non-price tools instead of matching every cut.

en.title: Retail and channel management
en.short: Designing channels, managing conflict and coordination, and running store and online retail.

sections.heading: Channel design and selection
sections.text: A marketing channel is the set of interdependent firms that make a product available to buyers. Design begins with the service outputs customers want: lot size, waiting time, convenience, variety and support. The firm then sets channel objectives, lists alternatives and judges each on economic cost, control and flexibility. Selection considers coverage, member capabilities, cost to serve and fit with the brand. A start-up may choose one distributor; a large firm may use several.

sections.heading: Conflict and coordination
sections.text: Channel conflict is disagreement among members about goals, roles or rewards. Vertical conflict is between levels, such as a manufacturer and retailer; horizontal conflict is between firms at the same level; multichannel conflict arises when channels compete for the same buyers. Causes include unclear territories, price differences and conflicting targets. Coordination uses contracts, margin rules, joint planning and information sharing. A channel captain can lead. Supply chain coordination aligns product, information and cash flows. The bullwhip effect is the widening of demand swings up the chain; sharing point-of-sale data, vendor-managed inventory (VMI) and collaborative planning, forecasting and replenishment (CPFR) reduce it.

sections.heading: Retail marketing mix
sections.text: The retail mix covers assortment, price, location and access, promotion, store atmosphere, service and process. Category management runs each product category, such as drinks or snacks, as its own business with its own targets. Retailers choose a target shopper and position: discount, convenience, specialty or experience. Online retail adds search, payment, delivery, returns and trust. The mix must be consistent; a low-price promise needs low costs and simple service.

sections.heading: Store and online management
sections.text: Store managers control layout, visual merchandising, stock, staffing and shrinkage (loss from theft, damage or error). Online managers control site speed, product information, fulfilment, last-mile delivery and returns. Omnichannel retail integrates them: shared inventory, click-and-collect and consistent prices. Case: Ada Stores, a made-up grocer in Lagos, Nigeria, adds online ordering. It shares daily stock data with suppliers and sets a two-hour pick window. This cuts duplicate stock and improves availability, but it must train staff and measure picking errors.

keyPoints: Channel design starts from customer service outputs and compares alternatives on economics, control and flexibility.
Channel conflict can be vertical, horizontal or multichannel; coordination needs clear roles, contracts and shared information.
Supply chain coordination reduces the bullwhip effect through point-of-sale data sharing, VMI and CPFR.
The retail mix combines assortment, price, location, promotion, atmosphere, service and process.
Omnichannel retail integrates store and online inventory, fulfilment and pricing.
Store managers watch layout, stock and shrinkage; online managers watch fulfilment, delivery and returns.

en.title: Social marketing and behaviour change
en.short: Principles, behaviour change theories, segmentation, campaign design, ethics and evaluation for social good.

sections.heading: What social marketing is
sections.text: Social marketing applies commercial marketing ideas to encourage voluntary behaviour that benefits individuals and society, such as safer sex, vaccination or handwashing. It is not advertising alone. Core principles are audience orientation, exchange, competition and a planned mix. Exchange means the audience must see a benefit that outweighs the cost of changing. Competition means the appeal of the unhealthy or unsafe behaviour, and other barriers, must be understood. The marketer offers a product (the behaviour), a price (costs and sacrifices), a place (where the behaviour happens) and promotion (messages and channels).

sections.heading: Theories and segmentation
sections.text: Behaviour change theories guide messages. The theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen) says intention depends on attitude, subjective norms and perceived control. Social cognitive theory (Bandura) stresses self-efficacy, modelling and environment. The stages of change model (Prochaska and DiClemente) describes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance. Diffusion of innovations (Rogers) explains how new practices spread through opinion leaders and networks. Segmentation divides a population by behaviour, risk, beliefs, age, gender or location. A campaign may target young men with low perceived risk, or mothers who decide household hygiene.

sections.heading: Designing and evaluating
sections.text: Campaign design sets a clear behaviour goal, audience, exchange, channels and partners. A made-up case: a district wants more households to treat drinking water. Formative research (research with the audience before the campaign) finds cost and doubt are barriers. The campaign uses community meetings, radio and a subsidy, and trains local sellers. Evaluation uses process measures (reach, materials distributed), impact measures (beliefs, intention) and outcome measures (behaviour). In a survey of 1,000 households, safe treatment rose from 30% to 45%. The absolute change is 15 percentage points; relative change is 15 ÷ 30 = 50%. A control group strengthens attribution.

sections.heading: Ethics and limits
sections.text: Ethics require voluntary consent, truthful claims, privacy and respect. Avoid stigma, fear without support, and targeting vulnerable people unfairly. Check unintended harms. Social marketing cannot fix problems caused mainly by poverty, policy or access; it works best with supportive services and environments.

keyPoints: Social marketing aims to change voluntary behaviour for social benefit, not to sell goods.
Exchange and competition explain why the audience would change and what competes with the desired behaviour.
Theory of planned behaviour, social cognitive theory, stages of change and diffusion of innovations guide campaign design.
