Segmentation groups audiences by behaviour, risk and beliefs so messages fit.
Evaluation separates process, impact and outcome measures; a control group helps attribution.
Ethics require consent, truthfulness, privacy and attention to unintended harm.

en.title: The marketing plan project
en.short: Building a marketing plan: analysis, objectives, mix, budget, control and presentation.

sections.heading: Plan and analysis
sections.text: A marketing plan is a written argument for marketing actions. It states the market, the evidence, the choices and the expected result. Begin with an executive summary, then a situation analysis: a structured review of customers, competitors, the company and the wider environment. SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats) and PESTLE (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental) are common tools. Keep the analysis short and link each finding to a decision.

sections.heading: Objectives and choices
sections.text: Objectives state what the plan will achieve, for whom and by when. Make them measurable: sales, market share, awareness or trial. Use the segmentation, targeting and positioning work already done; record the chosen target segment and position rather than repeating the theory. Then show how each element of the marketing mix (product, price, place, promotion; plus people, process and physical evidence for services) supports that position. Every choice should answer a finding from the analysis.

sections.heading: Budget and control
sections.text: The budget turns actions into money. List each activity, its cost and expected result. A made-up plan has ₦2,000,000: digital 50% = ₦1,000,000; events 25% = ₦500,000; print 15% = ₦300,000; research and measurement 10% = ₦200,000. Check: 1,000,000 + 500,000 + 300,000 + 200,000 = ₦2,000,000. For a target of 400 new customers, planned cost per acquisition = 2,000,000 ÷ 400 = ₦5,000. If first-year contribution (revenue minus variable costs) per customer is ₦8,000, expected contribution = 400 × 8,000 = ₦3,200,000, leaving ₦1,200,000 after the budget. Control compares actual results with targets at review points and triggers corrective action.

sections.heading: Implementation and presentation
sections.text: Implementation sets dates, owners, resources and dependencies. A timeline or Gantt chart shows who does what and when. Control needs metrics, review dates and decision rules: if cost per acquisition exceeds ₦5,000 by an agreed margin, change the channel mix. The presentation should tell one clear story: the problem, evidence, chosen target and position, mix, budget, risks and the decision requested. Put detail in appendices and keep the main slides simple.

keyPoints: A marketing plan links evidence to choices, actions, budget and control.
Situation analysis reviews customers, competitors, the company and the environment, and each finding should lead to a decision.
Objectives should be measurable and time-bound.
The plan records the chosen target segment and position and shows how the mix supports it.
Planned cost per acquisition = total marketing budget ÷ target number of new customers.
Implementation assigns dates and owners, control compares actual results with targets, and the presentation tells one clear story.

en.title: Advanced marketing theory: paradigms and debates
en.short: Exchange, relationship, service-dominant, institutional and critical views, and their research implications.

sections.heading: Paradigms and exchange
sections.text: Marketing theory is not one settled body. Exchange theory treats marketing as a voluntary transfer of value between two or more parties, each expecting gain. It gives a simple unit of analysis, the transaction, but critics say it can ignore power, trust and social context. Relationship marketing moves the focus from single transactions to ongoing ties, arguing that retention and cooperation can be more profitable. The debate is whether relationships are always worth their cost and how they should be measured.

sections.heading: Service and institutions
sections.text: Service-dominant logic (SDL), associated with Vargo and Lusch, argues that service, not goods, is the basis of exchange. Value is co-created with customers, and operant resources such as knowledge and skills matter more than operand resources such as raw materials. Critics ask for stronger empirical tests and warn against using SDL as a catch-all. Institutional theory explains how marketing practices spread because firms seek legitimacy, not only efficiency. Coercive, normative and mimetic pressures can make a practice standard across an industry.

sections.heading: Critical marketing and research
sections.text: Critical marketing questions managerial assumptions. It asks who gains and who loses from marketing, and examines consumerism, sustainability, power and ethics. It does not reject marketing but insists that research reflect on its own values. For a master’s researcher, these paradigms shape the research question, unit of analysis and method. A study of loyalty should say whether it treats loyalty as a transaction pattern, a relationship, a co-created experience or a legitimacy-driven practice. Context matters: a made-up Lagos bank may copy a rival’s loyalty app under mimetic pressure, while SDL would study how customers actually use it to create value. Critical marketing would ask whether the app helps customers or merely locks them in.

keyPoints: Exchange theory analyses marketing as voluntary value transfer, but may underplay power and context.
Relationship marketing shifts focus to ongoing ties and retention; costs and benefits are debated.
Service-dominant logic says service is the basis of exchange and value is co-created; it needs empirical testing.
Institutional theory explains practice diffusion through legitimacy and coercive, normative and mimetic pressures.
Critical marketing examines power, ethics and sustainability and asks who benefits.
Paradigm choice shapes research questions, constructs and methods.

en.title: Advanced consumer behaviour
en.short: Information processing, attitudes, culture, social identity, decision making and methods for studying consumers.

sections.heading: Processing and attitudes
sections.text: Consumers rarely process every message fully. The Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty and Cacioppo) separates a central route, where people think carefully about arguments, from a peripheral route, where cues such as source attractiveness or repetition shape judgement. The heuristic-systematic model (Chaiken) makes a similar distinction. Attention is selective and memory is reconstructive. An attitude is an evaluation of an object. Multi-attribute models, such as Fishbein’s, treat attitude as beliefs about attributes weighted by evaluation. The Theory of Planned Behaviour (Ajzen) adds subjective norms and perceived behavioural control as predictors of intention. Decisions use rules: compensatory rules trade a weak attribute against a strong one; non-compensatory rules, such as conjunctive (a cut-off on each attribute) or lexicographic (choose the best on the most important attribute), do not let a weakness be offset. Prospect theory (Kahneman and Tversky) shows losses loom larger than gains and framing changes choice.

sections.heading: Culture and identity
sections.text: Culture is the learned values, norms and meanings shared by a group. Consumer culture theory studies how consumption carries meaning through rituals and brand communities. Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner) holds that people define themselves partly through group membership, so reference groups and in-group favouritism shape preferences. A fictional case: Amina, a graduate student in Kano, buys a locally made skincare brand rather than a cheaper imported one because her friendship group values local production. The choice signals identity, not only price. Acculturation matters when consumers move between cultures.

sections.heading: Studying consumers
sections.text: Methods must match the question. Experiments test cause and effect by manipulating one or more factors. Surveys measure self-reports but suffer social desirability bias. Ethnography observes consumers in their setting; netnography (Kozinets) applies this to online communities. Diary studies capture behaviour over time. Eye tracking and implicit measures such as the Implicit Association Test probe processes people cannot report. Triangulation, using more than one method, strengthens claims. Ethical consent and privacy are essential, especially with digital data.

keyPoints: The Elaboration Likelihood Model separates central and peripheral routes to persuasion.
Attitudes can be modelled as weighted beliefs, and the Theory of Planned Behaviour adds norms and perceived control.
Compensatory and non-compensatory rules describe how consumers simplify choice.
Prospect theory shows that losses and framing affect decisions.
Culture and social identity shape consumption as meaning and group membership.
Methods range from experiments and surveys to ethnography, netnography and implicit measures.

en.title: Strategic brand management
en.short: Advanced brand strategy, equity models, architecture, global brands, valuation and research.

sections.heading: Strategy and equity models
sections.text: Advanced brand strategy treats the brand as an asset whose value comes from customer beliefs and behaviour. Aaker’s model lists five equity assets: awareness, perceived quality, associations, loyalty and proprietary assets such as trademarks. Keller’s customer-based brand equity (CBBE) pyramid runs from salience to performance and imagery, then judgements and feelings, and finally resonance. These models guide positioning and investment, but they are diagnostic, not a single score.

sections.heading: Architecture and global management
sections.text: Brand architecture is the way a firm organises brands and their relationships. A branded house uses one master brand, as with Virgin. A house of brands keeps separate brands, as Procter & Gamble often does. Endorsed brands link a product brand to a parent, while hybrid models mix these forms. In global brand management, firms choose between standardisation, which keeps one identity worldwide, and adaptation, which adjusts to local culture, language and regulation. The usual answer is a glocal compromise: a consistent core with local execution.

sections.heading: Valuation with worked example
sections.text: Brand valuation estimates a brand’s monetary worth. ISO 10668 sets out cost, market and income approaches. The income approach often uses royalty relief: estimate the royalty the firm would pay to license the brand, tax it, then discount it. Example: branded sales are ₦500m, the royalty rate is 5%, tax is 25%, and the discount rate is 12% with no growth. Royalty saving = 500m × 5% = 25m. After tax = 25m × (1 − 0.25) = 18.75m. Value = 18.75m ÷ 0.12 = ₦156.25m. The result depends on assumptions, so test them.

sections.heading: Research issues
sections.text: Research issues include measuring equity validly, separating brand effects from price and distribution, and ensuring cross-cultural equivalence of survey items. Digital data add behavioural signals but also noise and privacy limits. Triangulate surveys, sales data and experiments, and report uncertainty.

keyPoints: Brand equity is an intangible asset built from customer beliefs and behaviour.
Aaker’s five equity assets and Keller’s CBBE pyramid are diagnostic models, not single scores.
Brand architecture choices include branded house, house of brands, endorsed and hybrid forms.
Global brands usually standardise a core identity and adapt execution locally.
Royalty relief value = after-tax royalty saving ÷ discount rate when no growth is assumed.
Valuation and research results depend on assumptions and cross-cultural validity.

en.title: Research methods for a marketing dissertation
en.short: Philosophy, design, measurement, sampling, analysis, ethics and dissertation writing for marketing research.

sections.heading: Philosophy and design
sections.text: Research philosophy concerns ontology (what exists) and epistemology (how we can know). Positivism tests hypotheses with measurable data; interpretivism explores meanings; pragmatism chooses the approach that answers the question. The design follows: exploratory, descriptive or causal; cross-sectional or longitudinal; survey, experiment, case study or secondary data. Justify choices against the research question, not fashion. A methodology chapter explains these choices and their limits.

sections.heading: Measurement and sampling
sections.text: Measurement turns concepts into variables. Define each construct (the concept you measure), then check validity (measures the right concept) and reliability (consistent). Scales are nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio; Likert items are ordinal. Probability sampling needs a sampling frame (a list of the population). Probability methods (simple random, stratified, cluster), where each member has a known chance of selection, support generalisation; non-probability methods (convenience, purposive, quota) do not. For a 95% confidence interval and 5% margin of error with p = 0.5: n = (1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5) ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so 385. Adjust for small populations and non-response.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text: Qualitative analysis codes transcripts into themes; thematic analysis is common. Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics, then inferential tests or regression. Mixed methods combine both when the question needs breadth and depth. Report effect sizes (the size of a difference or relationship) and limitations. Ethics require informed consent, anonymity or confidentiality, no harm, secure data, and approval from your institution’s ethics committee; data protection law differs by country. Avoid fabricated data and fishing for significant results.

sections.heading: Writing it up
sections.text: Structure: introduction with gap and question, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and limitations. Keep an audit trail. Reference consistently in the required style. A dissertation is an argument: every method choice should answer the question and every claim should be evidenced. Write plainly, define technical terms and show how the findings answer the question.

keyPoints: Research philosophy shapes what counts as evidence; state your ontology and epistemology.
Design must follow the research question, not convenience.
Validity means measuring the right concept; reliability means measuring it consistently.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling does not.
For a proportion, n = z² p(1 − p) ÷ e²; at 95% confidence, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05, n = 385.
Ethics approval, informed consent and secure data are required; write an evidenced argument, not a description.
